method: soil-moisture-triggered irrigation inside the same Wofost72_WLP_FD engine the rainfed regions use, applied by runner.IrrigationController from inside the engine's daily rate step: on every day the profile is at or below trigger_depletion_fraction of its plant-available water, i.e. at SM = SMW + (1 - trigger_depletion_fraction) x (SMFCF - SMW) from this region's soils.csv row, it applies min(irrigation_amount_cm, capacity_cm_day_gross, allocation remaining), at most once a day. The water balance stays live, so a drought still shows a signal here; a potential-production run would erase it. irrigation_amount_cm is the GROSS application depth in CENTIMETRES -- the depth the system applies, which is what extension application-depth guidance states. PCSE reads it as the irrigate signal's 'amount' and adds amount x efficiency to the soil, so at 2.54 cm gross and 0.85 efficiency the profile receives 2.159 cm net per application. Supply is limited by a pumping-capacity ceiling and, where the governing district sets one, a seasonal allocation cap: see limits_method. Still unmodelled: projected aquifer decline, historical changes to rules and wells, surface water, and any rationing strategy. See README
source: management-allowed depletion of 50 percent of plant-available water, and centre-pivot application efficiency of 85 to 90 percent: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension NebGuide G1850, Irrigation Management for Corn; application depth 0.75 to 1.3 inches for medium- and fine-textured soils, same publication, with 1.0 inch = 2.54 cm taken as the mid-range increment; 0.85 as the centre-pivot efficiency assumed for general planning purposes: K-State Research and Extension L915, Using Evapotranspiration Reports for Center Pivot Irrigation Scheduling
limits_method: Pumping-capacity ceiling: G1851's minimum net design capacity for loam, silt loam and very fine sandy loam over a silt loam subsoil (2.5 in/ft plant-available water, this region's soils.csv texture) in Region 1, which meets corn water needs in nine years out of ten: 3.85 net gpm/ac. Howard County, where node 1's stratum point lies (41.1699 N, -98.6459 W), is in Region 1 on G1851's Figure 1: the dividing line crosses that latitude near -99.7 W. Conversion: 1 acre-inch = 43,560 ft2 x (1/12) ft x 7.48052 gal/ft3 = 27,154 US gal, so 1 gpm/ac pumped for 24 h = 1,440 gal/ac/day = 0.05303 in/day = 0.13470 cm/day. G1851's Table I figure is a net rate of continuous operation (its worked example scales it by 168 / (168 - downtime hours) to size a pump that runs less), so it converts directly with no pumping-hours factor; dividing by efficiency makes it the GROSS depth PCSE's 'amount' takes. 3.85 x 0.13470 = 0.5186 cm/day net / 0.85 = 0.6101 cm/day gross. A design MINIMUM: many real wells exceed it, so modelled stress is if anything overstated; a 2008 standard also embodies no aquifer decline since. Allocation cap: none. The point lies in the Lower Loup NRD, which meters use and limits NEW irrigated acres ('groundwater acres allocations') but sets no per-acre pumping allocation; the caps that do bind in Nebraska (Upper Republican, Lower Republican, North Platte NRDs) lie far west of this point.
limits_source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension NebGuide G1851, Minimum Center Pivot Design Capacities in Nebraska (Kranz, Martin, Irmak, van Donk and Yonts, issued May 2008), Table I and Figure 1; Table I data from von Bernuth, Martin, Gilley and Watts (1984), Irrigation System Capacities for Corn Production in Nebraska, Transactions of the ASAE 27(2): 419-428; NRD at the point: Nebraska state GIS layer NaturalResourcesDistrictBoundaries (gis.ne.gov), queried 2026-09-26; allocation rules: Lower Loup NRD, 2025 Lower Platte River Basin Coalition annual report (dated 2026-03-01), sections Flow Meter Data and Groundwater Acres Allocations

limits_method: Pumping-capacity ceiling: BORROWED. No K-State design-minimum capacity table exists (K-State MF2870 surveys nozzle packages, MF3066 states demand of 5 to 7.5 gpm/ac, and Lamm et al. 2007 relate yield to capacity), so this uses G1851's Nebraska standard as a labelled analogue: silt loam (2.5 in/ft) in Region 2, the western region whose eastern edge has 20-24 in of annual rainfall, closest to Hodgeman County's about 22 in: 4.62 net gpm/ac. Kansas's peak ET is higher than western Nebraska's, so this understates Kansas need and stays a minimum, biased toward stress like Nebraska's. Conversion: 1 acre-inch = 43,560 ft2 x (1/12) ft x 7.48052 gal/ft3 = 27,154 US gal, so 1 gpm/ac pumped for 24 h = 1,440 gal/ac/day = 0.05303 in/day = 0.13470 cm/day. G1851's Table I figure is a net rate of continuous operation (its worked example scales it by 168 / (168 - downtime hours) to size a pump that runs less), so it converts directly with no pumping-hours factor; dividing by efficiency makes it the GROSS depth PCSE's 'amount' takes. 4.62 x 0.13470 = 0.6223 cm/day net / 0.85 = 0.7321 cm/day gross. Allocation cap: none. Node 1's stratum point (38.1752 N, -99.7654 W) lies in Hodgeman County, outside every Groundwater Management District (GMD 3 removed Hodgeman on 1988-12-20), so no LEMA applies. The Pawnee Valley IGUCA limits NEW appropriations (750 acre-feet per 2-mile circle since 1985), not seasonal pumping on existing rights; water-right authorized quantities are per-right entitlements and out of scope.
limits_source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension NebGuide G1851, Minimum Center Pivot Design Capacities in Nebraska (Kranz, Martin, Irmak, van Donk and Yonts, issued May 2008), Table I and Figure 1; Table I data from von Bernuth, Martin, Gilley and Watts (1984), Irrigation System Capacities for Corn Production in Nebraska, Transactions of the ASAE 27(2): 419-428, applied to Kansas as a labelled analogue (plan 0003, R-1 option 1); GMD at the point: Kansas Geoportal layer Groundwater Management Districts (GMD), queried 2026-09-26, returning no district (a control point at Garden City returns GMD 3); Southwest Kansas GMD 3 boundary history; Big Bend GMD 5, Pawnee Valley IGUCA page; K-State Research and Extension MF2870 (2009) and MF3066; Lamm, Stone and O'Brien (2007), Applied Engineering in Agriculture 23(6)
